`RESULTS.json` is written:

```json
{
  "category_totals_eur": {
    "hardware": 8874.09, "meals": 2541.26, "office": 1775.45,
    "software": 9702.03, "training": 8992.94, "travel": 12137.98
  },
  "q2_total_eur": 44023.75,
  "mom_may_pct": 9.8,
  "mom_jun_pct": 10.0,
  "largest_txn_eur": 1312.26,
  "mean_txn_eur": 366.86,
  "travel_share_pct": 27.6,
  "over_budget": ["software", "travel"]
}
```

**Method.** Each transaction converted at its `rates.csv` rate and rounded to the cent (half-up, via `Decimal`) *before* summing, per the stated convention. Money to the cent, percentages to one decimal.

**Data check.** 120 rows, all dated in Q2 2026, no negatives, no duplicate IDs, no malformed rows. All six transaction categories appear in `budget.yaml` and all three currencies appear in `rates.csv` — no unmatched keys either direction.

**Verification.** I recomputed everything with an independent awk implementation; every figure matched. Worth noting: the CSV has CRLF line endings, which silently broke the first awk pass (the trailing `\r` made `$6=="USD"` fail, so USD rows fell through to the GBP rate and reported a wrong "largest transaction" of 1625.63). Python's csv reader handles this correctly, so the results were never affected — but it's a live trap for any shell-based tooling you point at this file. Two transactions (T0067, T0078) land on an exact half-cent; both round up under the half-up convention.

Monthly totals behind the MoM figures: April 13,316.21 → May 14,623.21 → June 16,084.33. June's +9.99% rounds to 10.0. Over budget: travel (12,137.98 vs 10,300) and software (9,702.03 vs 8,200).
